papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify and prune neurons responsible for copying bias in in-context learning, which improves performance across various tasks and models without task-specific data or fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Targeted neuron pruning mitigates copying bias and improves in-context learning performance across diverse tasks and models, offering a practical post-processing step for deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Copying errors are a significant source of errors in few-shot in-context learning, especially in smaller models.
Neurons responsible for copying behavior can be identified using Integrated Gradients on a synthetic vowel-counting task.
Pruning these identified neurons consistently improves in-context learning performance across a wide range of tasks and model architectures.
Pruning enhances the quality of task vectors, indicating improved task recognition and representation.
The method is practical as it uses a single synthetic task for neuron identification and does not require task-specific data.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive few-shot in-context learning (ICL) abilities. Still, we show that they are sometimes prone to a `copying bias', where they copy answers from provided examples instead of learning the underlying patterns. In this work, we propose a novel and simple method to mitigate such copying bias. First, we create a synthetic task and use the Integrated Gradients method to identify neurons that prioritize copying over generalization. We demonstrate that pruning these neurons consistently improves performance across a diverse set of ICL tasks. We also show that our method is applicable across various LLM architectures, including Transformers and State-Space Models, without requiring modifications. In our analysis, we adopt a task-recognition perspective on ICL and examine task vectors (Hendel et al., 2023) induced by the model. We find that pruning enhances the quality of these vectors, suggesting that the pruned neurons previously hindered effective task recognition.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning via Supportive Pretraining Data
papers.research_question: What makes certain pretraining data supportive for in-context learning, and what are the characteristics of such data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a gradient-based method (ORCA-ICL) to identify a small subset of pretraining data that supports in-context learning and analyzes the characteristics of this supportive data.
papers.conclusion: The work takes a first step towards understanding in-context learning by analyzing instance-level pretraining data, and the findings may guide future pretraining data construction to actively improve models' in-context learning performance.
papers.key_findings:
The supportive pretraining data for in-context learning do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks compared to random pretraining data.
The supportive pretraining data contain a relatively higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens.
The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from incorporating long-range context is below average, indicating that learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages in-context learning.
A continued pretraining on the identified supportive subset significantly improves the model's in-context learning ability, by up to 18%, without improving zero-shot performance.
The cross-task effectiveness of the supportive data suggests that part of the in-context learning behavior is task-specific and not universal across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The supportive pretraining data are identified with respect to the current language model checkpoint, and early checkpoints might have different supportive data.
The ORCA-ICL method is computationally expensive due to its gradient-based nature and the large size of pretraining data.
future_direction: Convert the correlational findings to causal ones to actively refine or construct pretraining data for improved in-context learning.
Apply the ORCA-ICL method to generation tasks in addition to classification tasks.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) improves language models' performance on a variety of NLP tasks by simply demonstrating a handful of examples at inference time. It is not well understood why ICL ability emerges, as the model has never been specifically trained on such demonstrations. Unlike prior work that explores implicit mechanisms behind ICL, we study ICL via investigating the pretraining data. Specifically, we first adapt an iterative, gradient-based approach to find a small subset of pretraining data that supports ICL. We observe that a continued pretraining on this small subset significantly improves the model's ICL ability, by up to 18%. We then compare the supportive subset constrastively with random subsets of pretraining data and discover: (1) The supportive pretraining data to ICL do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks. (2) The supportive pretraining data have a higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens. (3) The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from long-range context is below average, indicating learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages ICL. Our work takes a first step towards understanding ICL via analyzing instance-level pretraining data. Our insights have a potential to enhance the ICL ability of language models by actively guiding the construction of pretraining data in the future.

papers.title: Towards Understanding How Transformers Learn In-context Through a Representation Learning Lens
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) in Transformers work? Can ICL be related to gradient descent under the softmax attention setting without specific constructions for model weights and input tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the ICL inference process of a softmax attention layer is equivalent to gradient descent on a dual model, provides a representation learning interpretation, derives a generalization bound, and proposes attention modifications inspired by contrastive learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that ICL can be understood as gradient descent on a dual model from a representation learning perspective, and that attention modifications inspired by this view show promise in enhancing model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The ICL inference of a softmax attention layer is equivalent to one step of gradient descent on a dual model with a loss function that maximizes similarity between value-projected and key-projected tokens.
The dual model's training resembles a self-supervised representation learning process, analogous to contrastive learning without negative samples.
A generalization error bound for ICL is derived, showing the error decreases with the number of demonstration tokens.
The equivalence extends to a full Transformer layer (with FFN) and multiple attention layers.
Attention modifications inspired by representation learning (regularization, data augmentation, negative samples) can improve model performance on synthetic and GLUE tasks.
papers.limitation:
The negative sample selection method is too coarse and not always effective.
The attention modifications are tested on limited tasks and may not generalize.
future_direction: Develop more task-specific augmentation strategies for attention.
Design more effective methods for constructing negative samples in the attention mechanism.
Apply the representation learning lens to other model components and settings.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models based on Transformers have demonstrated remarkable in-context learning (ICL) abilities. With just a few demonstration examples, the models can implement new tasks without any parameter updates. However, it is still an open question to understand the mechanism of ICL. In this paper, we attempt to explore the ICL process in Transformers through a lens of representation learning. Initially, leveraging kernel methods, we figure out a dual model for one softmax attention layer. The ICL inference process of the attention layer aligns with the training procedure of its dual model, generating token representation predictions that are equivalent to the dual model's test outputs. We delve into the training process of this dual model from a representation learning standpoint and further derive a generalization error bound related to the quantity of demonstration tokens. Subsequently, we extend our theoretical conclusions to more complicated scenarios, including one Transformer layer and multiple attention layers. Furthermore, drawing inspiration from existing representation learning methods especially contrastive learning, we propose potential modifications for the attention layer. Finally, experiments are designed to support our findings.

papers.title: Inference and Verbalization Functions During In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do large language models perform in-context learning with irrelevant label words? The paper hypothesizes that they use separate inference and verbalization functions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes and empirically validates that large language models perform in-context learning via two sequential functions: an inference function that solves the task and a verbalization function that maps the answer to the label space, with inference invariant to label remapping.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that LMs use separate inference and verbalization functions during ICL, with inference invariant to label changes, and these functions are localized in model layers.
papers.key_findings:
Inference function is invariant to remappings of the label space.
Verbalization function maps answer representations to label words.
The two functions are localized in specific layers of the model.
These findings generalize across multiple models, datasets, and tasks.
The localization is consistent across different settings.
papers.limitation:
Alternative explanations exist, such as the intervened model ignoring plugged-in representations and re-solving the task.
Experiments filter out cases with low ICL accuracy, which may limit generalizability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LMs) are capable of in-context learning from a few demonstrations (example-label pairs) to solve new tasks during inference. Despite the intuitive importance of high-quality demonstrations, previous work has observed that, in some settings, ICL performance is minimally affected by irrelevant labels (Min et al., 2022). We hypothesize that LMs perform ICL with irrelevant labels via two sequential processes: an inference function that solves the task, followed by a verbalization function that maps the inferred answer to the label space. Importantly, we hypothesize that the inference function is invariant to remappings of the label space (e.g., "true"/"false" to "cat"/"dog"), enabling LMs to share the same inference function across settings with different label words. We empirically validate this hypothesis with controlled layer-wise interchange intervention experiments. Our findings confirm the hypotheses on multiple datasets and tasks (natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and topic classification) and further suggest that the two functions can be localized in specific layers across various open-sourced models, including GEMMA-7B, MISTRAL-7B-V0.3, GEMMA-2-27B, and LLAMA-3.1-70B.

papers.title: Beyond Induction Heads: In-Context Meta Learning Induces Multi-Phase Circuit Emergence
papers.research_question: How is meta-learning ability in in-context learning acquired during training, specifically through the dynamics of the model's internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-learning ability in in-context learning is acquired through multiple phases, each with a distinct circuit emerging, contrasting with the single-phase change observed in induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Multi-phase circuit emergence underlies the acquisition of meta-learning capabilities in in-context learning, and these findings help bridge the gap between controlled mechanistic interpretability experiments and practical large language model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model undergoes three learning phases (Non-Context, Semi-Context, Full-Context) with distinct circuits emerging in each phase.
Sudden jumps in accuracy align with the abrupt emergence of these circuits.
The Semi-Context Circuit explains the random-label robustness phenomenon observed in large language models.
In multi-head settings, circuits emerge in parallel, leading to smoother accuracy improvements while hidden circuit changes still occur.
Similar circuit patterns (chunk example in early layers, label attention in later layers) are observed in pretrained models like GPT2-XL on real-world tasks.
papers.limitation: The work uses a simplified transformer model and synthetic data, which may not fully capture the complexity of real large language model behaviors.
future_direction: Connecting controlled experiments in mechanistic interpretability to realistic use-cases of large language models.
Bridging geometric perspectives (like Local Learning Coefficient) with mechanistic circuit analyses to enrich interpretability methodologies.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit In-Context Learning (ICL), where predictions are made adaptively based on context. While prior work links induction heads to ICL through a sudden jump in accuracy, this can only account for ICL when the answer is included within the context. However, an important property of practical ICL in large language models is the ability to meta-learn how to solve tasks from context, rather than just copying answers from context; how such an ability is obtained during training is largely unexplored. In this paper, we experimentally clarify how such meta-learning ability is acquired by analyzing the dynamics of the model's circuit during training. Specifically, we extend the copy task from previous research into an In-Context Meta Learning setting, where models must infer a task from examples to answer queries. Interestingly, in this setting, we find that there are multiple phases in the process of acquiring such abilities, and that a unique circuit emerges in each phase, contrasting with the single-phases change in induction heads. The emergence of such circuits can be related to several phenomena known in large language models, and our analysis lead to a deeper understanding of the source of the transformer's ICL ability.

papers.title: To Copy or Not to Copy: Copying Is Easier to Induce Than Recall
papers.research_question: Can the model’s choice of information be controlled by a targeted intervention?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an arbitration vector that isolates the control signal for choosing between parametric recall and contextual copying, and shows that injecting this vector can steer model behavior, with copying being easier to induce than recall.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that copying from context is easier to induce than recalling from parametric knowledge, revealing an asymmetry in the model's arbitration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
The arbitration vector extracted from residual stream centroids can steer behavior between Copy→Recall and Recall→Copy.
Copying is easier to induce than recall: Recall→Copy requires smaller scaling and works from multiple token positions, while Copy→Recall requires larger scaling and only works at the object token.
The steering effect is spatially localized: effective layers differ for the two directions.
The intervention causes changes in attention routing and MLP contributions, with successful jamming of attention to the context only when applied at the object token.
The model's fluency (perplexity) is maintained at moderate scaling but degrades at extreme scaling.
papers.abstract: Language models used in retrieval-augmented settings must arbitrate between parametric knowledge stored in their weights and contextual information in the prompt. This work presents a mechanistic study of that choice by extracting an \emph{arbitration vector} from model activations on a curated dataset designed to disentangle (i) irrelevant contexts that elicit parametric recall and (ii) relevant but false contexts that elicit copying. The vector is computed as the residual-stream centroid difference between these regimes across 27 relations, and is injected as an additive intervention at selected layers and token spans to steer behavior in two directions: Copy$\rightarrow$Recall (suppressing context use) and Recall$\rightarrow$Copy (inducing the model to copy any token from the context). Experiments on two architectures (decoder-only and encoder/decoder) and two open-domain QA benchmarks show consistent behavior shifts under moderate scaling while monitoring accuracy and fluency. Mechanistic analyses of attention routing, MLP contributions, and layer-wise probability trajectories reveal an asymmetry: inducing copying is an easy ``reactivation'' process that can be triggered at different locations in the input, while restoring recall is a ``suppression'' process that is more fragile and strongly tied to object-token interventions.

papers.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Does the gradient flow with respect to the cross-entropy loss converge during training? If yes, how does the limiting model perform in-context learning? How do the building blocks of the transformer model contribute to in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that gradient flow training of a two-layer transformer on n-gram Markov chains converges to a model that performs a generalized induction head mechanism, elucidating the roles of attention, FFN, and normalization in in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical understanding of how transformer building blocks collaborate to enable in-context learning via a generalized induction head mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient flow converges during training of the transformer on in-context learning of n-gram Markov chains.
The limiting model implements a generalized induction head mechanism that selects an information set based on modified chi-square mutual information.
The first attention layer acts as a copier, the feed-forward network with normalization acts as a selector, and the second attention layer acts as a classifier.
Training dynamics occur in three phases: FFN learns the potential parent set, first attention focuses on selected parents, and second attention parameter increases.
The generalized induction head mechanism emerges from the collaboration of all transformer building blocks.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a cornerstone of large language model (LLM) functionality, yet its theoretical foundations remain elusive due to the complexity of transformer architectures. In particular, most existing work only theoretically explains how the attention mechanism facilitates ICL under certain data models. It remains unclear how the other building blocks of the transformer contribute to ICL. To address this question, we study how a two-attention-layer transformer is trained to perform ICL on $n$-gram Markov chain data, where each token in the Markov chain statistically depends on the previous $n$ tokens. We analyze a sophisticated transformer model featuring relative positional embedding, multi-head softmax attention, and a feed-forward layer with normalization. We prove that the gradient flow with respect to a cross-entropy ICL loss converges to a limiting model that performs a generalized version of the induction head mechanism with a learned feature, resulting from the congruous contribution of all the building blocks. In the limiting model, the first attention layer acts as a $\mathit{copier}$, copying past tokens within a given window to each position, and the feed-forward network with normalization acts as a $\mathit{selector}$ that generates a feature vector by only looking at informationally relevant parents from the window. Finally, the second attention layer is a $\mathit{classifier}$ that compares these features with the feature at the output position, and uses the resulting similarity scores to generate the desired output. Our theory is further validated by experiments.

papers.title: The Atlas of In-Context Learning: How Attention Heads Shape In-Context Retrieval Augmentation
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models facilitate in-context retrieval augmentation for question answering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an attribution-based method to identify and categorize attention heads in LLMs into in-context and parametric heads, revealing their specialized roles in instruction comprehension and knowledge retrieval during in-context retrieval augmentation.
papers.conclusion: The work sheds light on the mechanism of in-context retrieval augmentation by mapping the functional roles of attention heads, paving the way for more transparent and trustworthy retrieval-augmented language models.
papers.key_findings:
An attribution-based method can reliably identify in-context heads (which process prompt information) and parametric heads (which store relational knowledge).
In-context heads specialize into task heads for instruction comprehension and retrieval heads for copying answers from context.
Function vectors extracted from these heads or modifications to their attention weights can induce specific, targeted functions and influence answer generation.
Ablation of identified heads causally affects model performance in open-book and closed-book question answering settings.
Retrieval heads can be used to trace the source of knowledge used during inference, providing a step towards transparent retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a few models and datasets, and the analysis focuses on a specific task (question answering).
The proposed source tracking probe is preliminary and may not be perfect.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other tasks and models.
Improve the source tracking mechanism for retrieval-augmented generation.
Explore the interaction between attention heads more deeply.
papers.abstract: Large language models are able to exploit in-context learning to access external knowledge beyond their training data through retrieval-augmentation. While promising, its inner workings remain unclear. In this work, we shed light on the mechanism of in-context retrieval augmentation for question answering by viewing a prompt as a composition of informational components. We propose an attribution-based method to identify specialized attention heads, revealing in-context heads that comprehend instructions and retrieve relevant contextual information, and parametric heads that store entities' relational knowledge. To better understand their roles, we extract function vectors and modify their attention weights to show how they can influence the answer generation process. Finally, we leverage the gained insights to trace the sources of knowledge used during inference, paving the way towards more safe and transparent language models.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: The representation landscape of few-shot learning and fine-tuning in large language models
papers.research_question: How do in-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) affect the geometry of the internal representations in large language models when solving the same question-answering task?
papers.core_contribution: ICL and SFT create very different internal representation structures in LLMs for the same task, with ICL forming semantically organized clusters in early layers and SFT forming sharper answer-encoding clusters in later layers.
papers.conclusion: Geometric analysis reveals a transition between layers encoding high-level semantic information and those generating answers, showing fine-tuning and few-shot learning take distinct approaches to extract information from LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Both few-shot learning and fine-tuning show a clear division between model layers, with a marked peak in intrinsic dimension and a sudden change in geometrical structure in the middle of the network.
Few-shot learning leads to semantically meaningful clustering of representations in early layers, organized hierarchically by subject.
Fine-tuning enhances the sharp emergence of clustered representations according to answer identity in the second half of the network.
The representation landscape of ICL is more interpretable in early layers, while SFT is fuzzier in early layers but develops better-defined answer-encoding peaks later.
The transition layer separates layers encoding high-level semantics from those involved in generating answers.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) are two common strategies for improving the performance of modern large language models (LLMs) on specific tasks. Despite their different natures, these strategies often lead to comparable performance gains. However, little is known about whether they induce similar representations inside LLMs. We approach this problem by analyzing the probability landscape of their hidden representations in the two cases. More specifically, we compare how LLMs solve the same question-answering task, finding that ICL and SFT create very different internal structures, in both cases undergoing a sharp transition in the middle of the network. In the first half of the network, ICL shapes interpretable representations hierarchically organized according to their semantic content. In contrast, the probability landscape obtained with SFT is fuzzier and semantically mixed. In the second half of the model, the fine-tuned representations develop probability modes that better encode the identity of answers, while the landscape of ICL representations is characterized by less defined peaks. Our approach reveals the diverse computational strategies developed inside LLMs to solve the same task across different conditions, allowing us to make a step towards designing optimal methods to extract information from language models.

papers.title: Parameters vs. Context: Fine-Grained Control of Knowledge Reliance in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained control over a language model's reliance on its internal parametric knowledge versus external retrieved context in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) scenarios, especially when conflicts arise?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CK-PLUG, a plug-and-play inference-time method that uses a novel Confidence Gain metric to detect knowledge conflicts and a single tuning parameter to adjust token probability distributions, enabling fine-grained control over a model's reliance on parametric versus contextual knowledge in RAG.
papers.conclusion: CK-PLUG provides an effective framework for fine-grained control over knowledge reliance in LLMs during RAG, enabling users to balance parametric and contextual knowledge based on scenario needs and improving overall generation reliability.
papers.key_findings:
CK-PLUG enables a wide range of control over knowledge reliance, e.g., adjusting the Memory Recall (MR) ratio from 9.89% to 71.93% on LLAMA3-8B, significantly deviating from the baseline of 42.09%.
In adaptive mode (without manual α setting), CK-PLUG consistently improves performance across six diverse RAG downstream tasks compared to standard RAG baselines.
The method uses a single parameter α for fine-grained control, with MR varying approximately linearly as α changes across different models.
An ablation study shows that the conflict detection module (ConD) is crucial; removing it leads to a noticeable decline in generation quality, especially under extreme modulation settings.
CK-PLUG effectively balances parametric and contextual knowledge, maintaining generation fluency and logical consistency while adjusting knowledge preference.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge. However, conflicts between parametric knowledge and retrieved context pose challenges, particularly when retrieved information is unreliable or the model's internal knowledge is outdated. In such cases, LLMs struggle to determine whether to rely more on their own parameters or the conflicted context. To address this, we propose **CK-PLUG**, a plug-and-play method for controlling LLMs' reliance on parametric and contextual knowledge. We introduce a novel knowledge consistency metric, Confidence Gain, which detects knowledge conflicts by measuring entropy shifts in token probability distributions after context insertion. CK-PLUG then enables fine-grained control over knowledge preference by adjusting the probability distribution of tokens with negative confidence gain through a single tuning parameter. Experiments demonstrate CK-PLUG's ability to significantly regulate knowledge reliance in counterfactual RAG scenarios while maintaining generation fluency and knowledge accuracy. For instance, on Llama3-8B, memory recall (MR) of RAG response can be adjusted within a broad range (9.9%-71.9%), compared to the baseline of 42.1%. Moreover, CK-PLUG supports adaptive control based on the model's confidence in both internal and external knowledge, achieving consistent performance improvements across various general RAG tasks. Our code is available at: $\href{https://github.com/byronBBL/CK-PLUG}{\text{this https URL}}$.

papers.title: Learning Task Representations from In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How can we develop a task representation in a principled manner that generalizes across modalities such as language and mathematical functions? How can this representation be leveraged to preserve task fidelity on downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an automated method for encoding task information in ICL prompts as a weighted sum of attention heads, which generalizes across text and regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Learnable Task Vector method effectively encodes task information from in-context demonstrations and generalizes across modalities, providing a principled and automated approach to task representation in ICL.
papers.key_findings:
Existing task vector methods (Function Vector, In-Context Vector) fail to generalize to regression tasks.
The proposed Learnable Task Vector (LTV) successfully extracts task-specific information and excels in both text and regression tasks.
LTV preserves task fidelity in out-of-distribution conditions (prompts longer than seen during pre-training).
The benefits of LTV come from effective task encoding, not fine-tuning, by aligning the distribution of the last hidden state with that of an optimally in-context-learned model.
LTV requires training on only a small portion of the OOD case to generalize effectively.
papers.limitation:
The method is not intended to directly address issues like length generalization.
LTV requires training on more examples to maintain performance in noisy regression settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in in-context learning (ICL), where models adapt to new tasks through example-based prompts without requiring parameter updates.However, understanding how tasks are internally encoded and generalized remains a challenge.To address some of the empirical and technical gaps in the literature, we introduce an automated formulation for encoding task information in ICL prompts as a function of attention heads within the transformer architecture.This approach computes a single task vector as a weighted sum of attention heads, with the weights optimized causally via gradient descent.Our findings show that existing methods fail to generalize effectively to modalities beyond text.In response, we also design a benchmark to evaluate whether a task vector can preserve task fidelity in functional regression tasks.The proposed method successfully extracts task-specific information from in-context demonstrations and excels in both text and regression tasks, demonstrating its generalizability across modalities.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Massive Values in Self-Attention Modules are the Key to Contextual Knowledge Understanding
papers.research_question: What is the role of massive values in self-attention queries and keys, and how do they contribute to contextual knowledge understanding versus parametric knowledge retrieval?
papers.core_contribution: Massive values in attention queries and keys are critical for contextual knowledge understanding, and their concentration is caused by Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE).
papers.conclusion: The findings shed new light on how queries and keys operate in LLMs and offer practical insights for model design and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Massive values are concentrated in specific regions of attention queries and keys exclusively in models with RoPE.
These massive values are critical for contextual knowledge understanding rather than parametric knowledge retrieval.
Quantization methods that protect massive values preserve contextual understanding capabilities.
The concentration of massive values is caused by RoPE and appears from the first layers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in contextual knowledge understanding. In this paper, we show that these concentrated massive values consistently emerge in specific regions of attention queries (Q) and keys (K) while not having such patterns in values (V) in various modern transformer-based LLMs (Q, K, and V mean the representations output by the query, key, and value layers respectively). Through extensive experiments, we further demonstrate that these massive values play a critical role in interpreting contextual knowledge (knowledge obtained from the current context window) rather than in retrieving parametric knowledge stored within the model's parameters. Our further investigation of quantization strategies reveals that ignoring these massive values leads to a pronounced drop in performance on tasks requiring rich contextual understanding, aligning with our analysis. Finally, we trace the emergence of concentrated massive values and find that such concentration is caused by Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE), which has appeared since the first layers. These findings shed new light on how Q and K operate in LLMs and offer practical insights for model design and optimization. The Code is Available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Rope_with_LLM.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: What Can Transformers Learn In-Context? A Case Study of Simple Function Classes
papers.research_question: Can we train a model to in-context learn a function class? What is the relationship between tasks on which in-context learning succeeds and the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can be trained from scratch to perform in-context learning of simple function classes (e.g., linear functions) with performance comparable to optimal estimators, and this ability generalizes under distribution shifts and extends to more complex function classes.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can encode complex learning algorithms for in-context learning of various function classes, generalizing under distribution shifts, and this work lays groundwork for future research on in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can be trained to in-context learn linear functions with error comparable to the optimal least squares estimator.
The trained model generalizes to out-of-distribution prompts, including shifts in input distributions, label noise, and mismatches between in-context examples and query inputs.
Transformers can in-context learn more complex function classes (sparse linear functions, two-layer neural networks, decision trees) with performance matching or exceeding specialized algorithms like Lasso or gradient descent.
Model capacity and problem dimensionality affect in-context learning performance; larger models handle higher dimensions and distribution shifts better.
Curriculum learning drastically speeds up training without significantly affecting final performance.
papers.limitation:
Understanding the implications of these results for large language models requires further investigation.
Model performance degrades under some distribution shifts, e.g., with skewed covariance or extreme scaling of prompt inputs.
future_direction: Investigating the complexity of in-context learning in terms of function class, model capacity, and training data.
Understanding why curriculum learning speeds up training and whether similar speedups are possible for large language models.
Comparing inductive biases of different model families (e.g., Transformers vs. LSTMs) for in-context learning.
papers.abstract: In-context learning refers to the ability of a model to condition on a prompt sequence consisting of in-context examples (input-output pairs corresponding to some task) along with a new query input, and generate the corresponding output. Crucially, in-context learning happens only at inference time without any parameter updates to the model. While large language models such as GPT-3 exhibit some ability to perform in-context learning, it is unclear what the relationship is between tasks on which this succeeds and what is present in the training data. To make progress towards understanding in-context learning, we consider the well-defined problem of training a model to in-context learn a function class (e.g., linear functions): that is, given data derived from some functions in the class, can we train a model to in-context learn "most" functions from this class? We show empirically that standard Transformers can be trained from scratch to perform in-context learning of linear functions -- that is, the trained model is able to learn unseen linear functions from in-context examples with performance comparable to the optimal least squares estimator. In fact, in-context learning is possible even under two forms of distribution shift: (i) between the training data of the model and inference-time prompts, and (ii) between the in-context examples and the query input during inference. We also show that we can train Transformers to in-context learn more complex function classes -- namely sparse linear functions, two-layer neural networks, and decision trees -- with performance that matches or exceeds task-specific learning algorithms. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/dtsip/in-context-learning .

papers.title: Provable In-Context Vector Arithmetic via Retrieving Task Concepts
papers.research_question: How does a non-linear residual transformer trained on QA data perform factual-recall in-context learning via vector arithmetic, and what are its advantages over Word2Vec?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a theoretical framework showing that transformers trained on QA data can perform factual-recall in-context learning via vector arithmetic, and proves that training on QA data enables task vector retrieval while training on ICL data leads to harmful memorization.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical results explain the advantages of transformers over Word2Vec in performing in-context vector arithmetic for factual recall, and are supported by empirical simulations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on QA data retrieve task vectors and achieve arbitrarily small test error on factual-recall ICL tasks.
Training on ICL data leads to harmful memorization of low-level features and fails to retrieve task vectors, resulting in constant test error.
Transformers can regress task vectors from demonstration pairs without requiring a query word.
Transformers generalize compositionally to unseen task prompts and distribution shifts by leveraging conic combinations of learned task vectors.
The theoretical analysis elucidates the advantages of transformers over static embedding methods like Word2Vec.
papers.limitation: The study is confined to single-token factual-recall ICL tasks and does not claim to be a universal explanation for how LLMs handle complex multi-token or factual tasks.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) has garnered significant attention for its ability to grasp functions/tasks from demonstrations. Recent studies suggest the presence of a latent task/function vector in LLMs during ICL. Merullo et al. (2024) showed that LLMs leverage this vector alongside the residual stream for Word2Vec-like vector arithmetic, solving factual-recall ICL tasks. Additionally, recent work empirically highlighted the key role of Question-Answer data in enhancing factual-recall capabilities. Despite these insights, a theoretical explanation remains elusive. To move one step forward, we propose a theoretical framework building on empirically grounded hierarchical concept modeling. We develop an optimization theory, showing how nonlinear residual transformers trained via gradient descent on cross-entropy loss perform factual-recall ICL tasks via vector arithmetic. We prove 0-1 loss convergence and show the strong generalization, including robustness to concept recombination and distribution shifts. These results elucidate the advantages of transformers over static embedding predecessors. Empirical simulations corroborate our theoretical insights.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: When Parts Are Greater Than Sums: Individual LLM Components Can Outperform Full Models
papers.research_question: How do individual components (attention heads and MLPs) behave in in-context learning, and can they outperform the full model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that individual attention heads and MLPs can have higher accuracy than the full model in ICL, and proposes component reweighting, a method to learn to scale component contributions from few-shot examples, improving ICL accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The decomposition provides a new perspective on ICL, revealing consistent component characteristics, and motivates a practical method (component reweighting) that improves ICL accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Good-performing components exist that individually outperform the full model on classification tasks.
Bad-performing components perform below chance accuracy.
Label-biased components always predict the same label regardless of input.
Component accuracies are consistent across different demonstration sets and contrastive templates.
Component reweighting, which learns to scale component contributions from few labeled examples, improves ICL accuracy over standard ICL.
papers.limitation:
Component reweighting requires a small set of labeled data for training the weights.
The method is only experimented with classification tasks, leaving generation tasks for future work.
The paper does not focus on circuits, so mechanistic understanding of components is limited.
future_direction: Generalize the method to generation tasks.
papers.abstract: This paper studies in-context learning by decomposing the output of large language models into the individual contributions of attention heads and MLPs (components). We observe curious components: good-performing ones that individually do well on a classification task, even when the model performs poorly; bad-performing ones that do much worse than chance; and label-biased components that always predict the same label. We find that component accuracies are well-correlated across different demonstration sets and perturbations of prompt templates. Based on our findings, we propose component reweighting, which learns to linearly re-scale the component activations from a few labeled examples. Given 24 labeled examples, our method improves by an average of 6.0% accuracy points over 24-shot ICL across 8 tasks on Llama-2-7B. Overall, this paper both enriches our understanding of ICL and provides a practical method for improvement by examining model internals.

papers.title: Diagnosing Knowledge Conflict in Multimodal Long-Chain Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in long chain-of-thought reasoning often fail when different knowledge sources provide conflicting signals. We formalize these failures under a unified notion of knowledge conflict, distinguishing input-level objective conflict from process-level effective conflict. Through probing internal representations, we reveal that: (I) Linear Separability: different conflict types are explicitly encoded as linearly separable features rather than entangled; (II) Depth Localization: conflict signals concentrate in mid-to-late layers, indicating a distinct processing stage for conflict encoding; (III) Hierarchical Consistency: aggregating noisy token-level signals along trajectories robustly recovers input-level conflict types; and (IV) Directional Asymmetry: reinforcing the model's implicit source preference under conflict is far easier than enforcing the opposite source. Our findings provide a mechanism-level view of multimodal reasoning under knowledge conflict and enable principled diagnosis and control of long-CoT failures.

papers.title: Unveiling Knowledge Utilization Mechanisms in LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge stream within the RAG framework, and how do LLM modules function in knowledge utilization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unveils the intrinsic knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLMs in RAG scenarios from macroscopic (knowledge streaming) and microscopic (module functions) perspectives, introducing KAPE to identify knowledge-specific neurons and demonstrating how deactivating them can shift the model's reliance between internal and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how LLMs integrate internal and external knowledge in RAG, advancing interpretability and paving the way for designing more efficient and controllable LLM architectures capable of balancing parametric and contextual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge streaming within RAG can be divided into four distinct stages: knowledge refinement, elicitation, expression, and contestation.
The relevance of retrieved passages guides the knowledge streaming, primarily affecting the knowledge elicitation stage.
The proposed KAPE metric can identify neurons associated with internal or external knowledge, and selectively deactivating these neurons can alter the LLM's preference for one knowledge source over the other.
Multi-head attention (MHA) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules have complementary roles: MHA facilitates information integration, while MLP layers help verify knowledge accuracy and are sensitive to factual correctness.
The LLM evaluates the relevance between the query and external knowledge during the knowledge elicitation stage via information flow between them.
future_direction: Future work will focus on refining these mechanisms to improve real-world applications and extend the boundaries of AI-driven knowledge retrieval systems, developing more nuanced models that better handle the complexities of knowledge integration.
papers.abstract: Considering the inherent limitations of parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely employed to expand their knowledge scope. Since RAG has shown promise in knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain question answering, its broader application to complex tasks and intelligent assistants has further advanced its utility. Despite this progress, the underlying knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLM-based RAG remain underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic investigation of the intrinsic mechanisms by which LLMs integrate internal (parametric) and external (retrieved) knowledge in RAG scenarios. Specially, we employ knowledge stream analysis at the macroscopic level, and investigate the function of individual modules at the microscopic level. Drawing on knowledge streaming analyses, we decompose the knowledge utilization process into four distinct stages within LLM layers: knowledge refinement, knowledge elicitation, knowledge expression, and knowledge contestation. We further demonstrate that the relevance of passages guides the streaming of knowledge through these stages. At the module level, we introduce a new method, knowledge activation probability entropy (KAPE) for neuron identification associated with either internal or external knowledge. By selectively deactivating these neurons, we achieve targeted shifts in the LLM's reliance on one knowledge source over the other. Moreover, we discern complementary roles for multi-head attention and multi-layer perceptron layers during knowledge formation. These insights offer a foundation for improving interpretability and reliability in retrieval-augmented LLMs, paving the way for more robust and transparent generative solutions in knowledge-intensive domains.

papers.title: In-Context Learning Strategies Emerge Rationally
papers.research_question: Why do models learn different strategies for in-context learning, and what drives the transition between memorizing and generalizing predictors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hierarchical Bayesian framework that explains and predicts in-context learning strategies as a tradeoff between loss and complexity, accurately modeling Transformer next-token predictions without access to model weights.
papers.conclusion: The hierarchical Bayesian framework provides a unifying explanatory and predictive account of in-context learning, suggesting the value of viewing learning behavior as a rational adaptation to data properties and computational constraints.
papers.key_findings:
Model behavior transitions between two Bayesian predictors: a memorizing predictor (discrete prior over seen tasks) and a generalizing predictor (continuous prior over true distribution).
The hierarchical Bayesian framework almost perfectly predicts Transformer next-token predictions throughout training without assuming access to its weights.
The framework explains ICL phenomena such as task diversity effects and transient generalization via a loss-complexity tradeoff.
The framework predicts a superlinear trend in the timescale for transitioning from generalization to memorization as task diversity increases.
The simplicity bias and power-law scaling of loss are key computational constraints that drive the tradeoff between strategies.
papers.limitation: The complexity measure used in the framework may not fully capture the Transformer's bias towards simpler solutions in certain conditions, such as low task diversity settings.
future_direction: Explaining in-context transitions of novel concepts or behaviors.
Applying the framework to other pretraining phenomena, such as learning heuristics vs. grammar in language modeling.
Connecting the top-down framework to bottom-up mechanistic accounts of how Transformers implement the loss-complexity tradeoff.
papers.abstract: Recent work analyzing in-context learning (ICL) has identified a broad set of strategies that describe model behavior in different experimental conditions. We aim to unify these findings by asking why a model learns these disparate strategies in the first place. Specifically, we start with the observation that when trained to learn a mixture of tasks, as is popular in the literature, the strategies learned by a model for performing ICL can be captured by a family of Bayesian predictors: a memorizing predictor, which assumes a discrete prior on the set of seen tasks, and a generalizing predictor, where the prior matches the underlying task distribution. Adopting the normative lens of rational analysis, where a learner's behavior is explained as an optimal adaptation to data given computational constraints, we develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework that almost perfectly predicts Transformer next-token predictions throughout training -- without assuming access to its weights. Under this framework, pretraining is viewed as a process of updating the posterior probability of different strategies, and inference-time behavior as a posterior-weighted average over these strategies' predictions. Our framework draws on common assumptions about neural network learning dynamics, which make explicit a tradeoff between loss and complexity among candidate strategies: beyond how well it explains the data, a model's preference towards implementing a strategy is dictated by its complexity. This helps explain well-known ICL phenomena, while offering novel predictions: e.g., we show a superlinear trend in the timescale for transitioning from generalization to memorization as task diversity increases. Overall, our work advances an explanatory and predictive account of ICL grounded in tradeoffs between strategy loss and complexity.

papers.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Why does in-context learning (ICL) emerge and then disappear (transience) during training, and what are the dynamics between ICL and other learning strategies?
papers.core_contribution: The transience of in-context learning (ICL) is explained by coopetition (cooperative and competitive dynamics) between ICL and a newly identified strategy called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), where shared sub-circuits enable ICL emergence before CIWL asymptotically dominates.
papers.conclusion: Strategy coopetition between ICL and CIWL explains the emergence and transience of ICL, providing a deeper mechanistic understanding of how capabilities dynamically trade off during transformer training.
papers.key_findings:
The asymptotic strategy after ICL transience is a hybrid called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), which depends on both in-weights information and the presence of the correct label in context.
ICL and CIWL share critical sub-circuits (e.g., Layer 2 induction heads), leading to cooperative dynamics that enable ICL emergence.
ICL emergence is only possible when CIWL is not fully formed, and ICL is faster to emerge but asymptotically dominated by CIWL.
A minimal mathematical model captures the coopetition dynamics and explains transience.
Matching context and query exemplars in the data can make ICL persistent by removing the asymptotic bias towards CIWL.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a powerful ability that emerges in transformer models, enabling them to learn from context without weight updates. Recent work has established emergent ICL as a transient phenomenon that can sometimes disappear after long training times. In this work, we sought a mechanistic understanding of these transient dynamics. Firstly, we find that, after the disappearance of ICL, the asymptotic strategy is a remarkable hybrid between in-weights and in-context learning, which we term "context-constrained in-weights learning" (CIWL). CIWL is in competition with ICL, and eventually replaces it as the dominant strategy of the model (thus leading to ICL transience). However, we also find that the two competing strategies actually share sub-circuits, which gives rise to cooperative dynamics as well. For example, in our setup, ICL is unable to emerge quickly on its own, and can only be enabled through the simultaneous slow development of asymptotic CIWL. CIWL thus both cooperates and competes with ICL, a phenomenon we term "strategy coopetition." We propose a minimal mathematical model that reproduces these key dynamics and interactions. Informed by this model, we were able to identify a setup where ICL is truly emergent and persistent.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Induction Heads for In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What are the precise training dynamics during the emergence of induction heads for in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a simple, interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing induction heads and proves that training dynamics are constrained to a low-dimensional subspace, with only three parameters accounting for the emergence.
papers.conclusion: This work shows how induction heads emerge in an ICL task and paves the way for a better theoretical understanding of transformer learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrices of an induction head have a simple structure described by three pseudo-parameters (α3, β2, γ3).
Training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace, and only three dimensions are necessary for the induction head to emerge.
The emergence time of the induction head is quadratic in the context length (Θ(N^2)).
The three parameters emerge in a specific order: γ first, then β, then α.
The emergence of the induction head is self-contained, unaided by the other parameters.
papers.limitation:
Architectural scope is limited to a disentangled, attention-only transformer; production models with LayerNorm, MLPs, and additive residual streams may have different dynamics.
Theoretical results assume orthonormal inputs and zero initialization, which may not hold in practice and could alter emergence times.
The study uses a simplified ICL task (exact matching of item-label pairs), not natural language with its complexities.
future_direction: Exploring how data distributional properties like burstiness modulate the effective context length and emergence.
Investigating other means of reducing effective context length, such as special positional embeddings.
Applying a similar approach to study other phenomena like the in-context vs. in-weights learning trade-off, abrupt learning, or other transformer circuits.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant architecture for natural language processing. Part of their success is owed to a remarkable capability known as in-context learning (ICL): they can acquire and apply novel associations solely from their input context, without any updates to their weights. In this work, we study the emergence of induction heads, a previously identified mechanism in two-layer transformers that is particularly important for in-context learning. We uncover a relatively simple and interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing the induction head. We theoretically explain the origin of this structure using a minimal ICL task formulation and a modified transformer architecture.
