We further validate that the same training dynamics observed in our controlled setting also arise during real-world language model pretraining, and we analyze how post-training procedures can reshape models' knowledge preferences. Together, our findings provide concrete empirical guidance for training language models that harmoniously integrate parametric and in-context knowledge.

papers.title: Analysing the Residual Stream of Language Models Under Knowledge Conflicts
papers.research_question: Can we identify the conflict between context and parameter knowledge by probing the residual stream? Can we know which source of knowledge the models will use before they generate the answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally register knowledge conflict signals in the residual stream, which can be detected by probing intermediate activations. The residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model relies on contextual versus parametric knowledge, enabling prediction of the model's knowledge selection behavior.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit internal mechanisms for identifying conflicts in the mid-layers, and the residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model uses context and parametric knowledge to predict. This analysis provides insights into the behaviour of LLMs in the presence of knowledge conflicts.
papers.key_findings:
The signal of knowledge conflict rises from intermediate layers (e.g., layer 13-14) and can be detected with high accuracy using linear probing.
The residual stream exhibits different skewness patterns (measured by Kurtosis, Hoyer, Gini) when the model uses contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge.
The decision of which knowledge to use occurs after the detection of the knowledge conflict signal.
The probing model's performance for conflict detection peaks around the 14th layer and then decreases slightly.
The skewness patterns are more pronounced in hidden states than in MLP or Self-Attention activations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context. Such conflicts can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can identify knowledge conflicts and whether it is possible to know which source of knowledge the model will rely on by analysing the residual stream of the LLM. Through probing tasks, we find that LLMs can internally register the signal of knowledge conflict in the residual stream, which can be accurately detected by probing the intermediate model activations. This allows us to detect conflicts within the residual stream before generating the answers without modifying the input or model parameters. Moreover, we find that the residual stream shows significantly different patterns when the model relies on contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge to resolve conflicts. This pattern can be employed to estimate the behaviour of LLMs when conflict happens and prevent unexpected answers before producing the answers. Our analysis offers insights into how LLMs internally manage knowledge conflicts and provides a foundation for developing methods to control the knowledge selection processes.

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we control the knowledge selection behavior of large language models (LLMs) when there is a conflict between their parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in the hidden states of LLMs, enabling precise control over knowledge selection behavior during inference to resolve context-memory conflicts.
papers.conclusion: SPARE provides an effective and efficient training-free method for controlling knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, offering a promising approach to managing knowledge conflicts without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected by probing the residual stream of LLMs, with the strongest signal appearing in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively steers LLMs to use either contextual or parametric knowledge, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
The residual stream exhibits a significantly more skewed representation when the model uses contextual knowledge compared to when it uses parametric knowledge.
SPARE requires editing only a very small set of SAE features (e.g., less than 0.05% for Gemma2-9B) to achieve control.
The method is more effective at changing the model's behavior from using contextual to parametric knowledge than other inference-time methods.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on pre-trained SAEs, so it may not apply to models where such SAEs are unavailable or cannot be efficiently trained.
The experiments are conducted on specific open-domain QA tasks; generalization to other task types (e.g., complex reasoning, long-form generation) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in a binary fashion (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), whereas real-world decisions may require more nuanced approaches.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context -- this phenomenon, known as \emph{context-memory knowledge conflicts}, can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. Analysing the internal activations of LLMs, we find that they can internally register the signals of knowledge conflict at mid-layers. Such signals allow us to detect whether a knowledge conflict occurs and use \emph{inference-time} intervention strategies to resolve it. In this work, we propose \textsc{SpARE}, a \emph{training-free} representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to control the knowledge selection behaviour of LLMs. \textsc{SpARE} identifies the functional features that control the knowledge selection behaviours and applies them to edit the internal activations of LLMs at inference time. Our experimental results show that \textsc{SpARE} can effectively control the usage of either knowledge source to resolve knowledge conflict in open-domain question-answering tasks, surpassing existing representation engineering methods ($+10\%$) as well as contrastive decoding methods ($+15\%$).

papers.title: Larger language models do in-context learning differently
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in language models interact with semantic priors versus input-label mappings, and how does this change with model scale and instruction tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The ability to override semantic priors and learn input-label mappings in-context emerges with model scale, and instruction tuning strengthens both semantic priors and input-label mapping learning, but more so the former.
papers.conclusion: Larger language models do in-context learning differently by being more capable of learning input-label mappings and overriding semantic priors, and instruction tuning further modulates these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Small language models rely heavily on semantic priors and cannot override them when presented with flipped labels in-context.
Large language models can override semantic priors and learn input-label mappings from flipped labels, causing performance to drop below random guessing.
The ability to perform in-context learning with semantically-unrelated labels (SUL-ICL) emerges with model scale, indicating that large models can learn input-label mappings without semantic cues.
Instruction tuning improves the ability to learn input-label mappings in SUL-ICL but also strengthens reliance on semantic priors, making instruction-tuned models less able to override priors with flipped labels.
Large language models can perform linear classification in a SUL-ICL setting, suggesting that the ability to learn input-label mappings extends to non-natural-language tasks.
papers.abstract: We study how in-context learning (ICL) in language models is affected by semantic priors versus input-label mappings. We investigate two setups-ICL with flipped labels and ICL with semantically-unrelated labels-across various model families (GPT-3, InstructGPT, Codex, PaLM, and Flan-PaLM). First, experiments on ICL with flipped labels show that overriding semantic priors is an emergent ability of model scale. While small language models ignore flipped labels presented in-context and thus rely primarily on semantic priors from pretraining, large models can override semantic priors when presented with in-context exemplars that contradict priors, despite the stronger semantic priors that larger models may hold. We next study semantically-unrelated label ICL (SUL-ICL), in which labels are semantically unrelated to their inputs (e.g., foo/bar instead of negative/positive), thereby forcing language models to learn the input-label mappings shown in in-context exemplars in order to perform the task. The ability to do SUL-ICL also emerges primarily with scale, and large-enough language models can even perform linear classification in a SUL-ICL setting. Finally, we evaluate instruction-tuned models and find that instruction tuning strengthens both the use of semantic priors and the capacity to learn input-label mappings, but more of the former.

papers.title: From Compression to Expression: A Layerwise Analysis of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs extract and differentiate task information from shallow to deep layers during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and analyzes the Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon in ICL, where early layers compress task information from demonstrations and later layers express it for prediction, with implications for performance and robustness.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a comprehensive analysis of ICL internal dynamics, uncovering the prevalent Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon, which deepens understanding of structured representation learning in LLMs and offers practical implications for interpretability, efficiency, and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
The Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon is prevalent across diverse model architectures (transformer and state-space) and task domains (symbolic, language, multimodal).
Larger models and more demonstrations lead to more compressed task representations, explaining performance improvements with scale and context length.
Noisy demonstrations result in less compressed representations, but ICL remains robust up to a certain noise ratio due to distinguishable task vectors.
Attention mechanisms contribute to reducing both bias and variance of task representations as the number of demonstrations increases, as shown in a theoretical analysis.
Task-vector contrastive fine-tuning, motivated by the analysis, can further compress task vectors and improve task-vector accuracy.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis uses a simplified linear attention model, sharing the same simplifications and limitations as prior work on linear self-attention.
future_direction: Theoretical investigation of the phenomenon in the infinite-sample regime.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to adapt to new tasks without weight updates by learning from demonstration sequences. While ICL shows strong empirical performance, its internal representational mechanisms are not yet well understood. In this work, we conduct a statistical geometric analysis of ICL representations to investigate how task-specific information is captured across layers. Our analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon, which we term *Layerwise Compression-Expression*: early layers progressively produce compact and discriminative representations that encode task information from the input demonstrations, while later layers express these representations to incorporate the query and generate the prediction. This phenomenon is observed consistently across diverse tasks and a range of contemporary LLM architectures. We demonstrate that it has important implications for ICL performance -- improving with model size and the number of demonstrations -- and for robustness in the presence of noisy examples. To further understand the effect of the compact task representation, we propose a bias-variance decomposition and provide a theoretical analysis showing how attention mechanisms contribute to reducing both variance and bias, thereby enhancing performance as the number of demonstrations increases. Our findings reveal an intriguing layerwise dynamic in ICL, highlight how structured representations emerge within LLMs, and showcase that analyzing internal representations can facilitate a deeper understanding of model behavior.

papers.title: Localizing Task Recognition and Task Learning in In-Context Learning via Attention Head Analysis
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models mechanistically implement in-context learning, specifically the components of task recognition and task learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in task recognition and task learning, providing a unified mechanistic account of in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The TSLA framework successfully localizes TR and TL components to specific attention heads, providing a unified mechanistic explanation of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
TR heads and induction heads are highly overlapping and correlated, indicating that induction heads primarily contribute to task recognition.
TR heads attend more to demonstration labels, while TL heads attend more to query tokens.
Ablating TR heads reduces both accuracy and TR ratio, while ablating TL heads reduces accuracy but not TR ratio.
TR heads align hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label.
The identified TR heads are consistent across tasks, while TL heads are more task-specific.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanistic underpinnings of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models by reconciling two dominant perspectives: the component-level analysis of attention heads and the holistic decomposition of ICL into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL). We propose a novel framework based on Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in TR and TL, and demonstrate their distinct yet complementary roles. Through correlation analysis, ablation studies, and input perturbations, we show that the identified TR and TL heads independently and effectively capture the TR and TL components of ICL. Using steering experiments with geometric analysis of hidden states, we reveal that TR heads promote task recognition by aligning hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label to facilitate prediction. We further show how previous findings on ICL mechanisms, including induction heads and task vectors, can be reconciled with our attention-head-level analysis of the TR-TL decomposition. Our framework thus provides a unified and interpretable account of how large language models execute ICL across diverse tasks and settings.

papers.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning, and what is the mechanistic basis of the abrupt transition observed during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that data distributional dependencies for in-context learning are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network, and that the abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, which is explained by a phenomenological model with nested logits.
papers.conclusion: The abrupt transition in ICL is due to the sequential learning of three nested logits in the induction head, and an intrinsic curriculum (slow learning of a simpler strategy) may be necessary to guide the network towards the ICL solution.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing burstiness (B) and number of classes (K) promotes ICL while decreasing IWL.
Within-class variation (ε) promotes ICL and decreases IWL.
A Zipfian rank-frequency distribution (α=1) promotes both ICL and IWL simultaneously.
The network can learn both ICL and IWL solutions simultaneously when trained on a mix of sequences.
The abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, preceded by a slow learning phase where the network learns to randomly pick a contextual label.
papers.limitation:
The model is minimal and larger models may use different mechanisms than the ones identified.
The analysis did not use heuristics such as weight tying, which are common in LLMs and might change the learning dynamics.
future_direction: Testing the hypothesis that learning of simpler ICL operations enables the learning of more complex ICL strategies in large language models.
Using methods for mechanistic interpretability to probe these mechanisms in LLMs.
Exploring the role of curricula for accelerating ICL in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer models exhibit in-context learning: the ability to accurately predict the response to a novel query based on illustrative examples in the input sequence. In-context learning contrasts with traditional in-weights learning of query-output relationships. What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning? Recent work has shown that specific distributional properties inherent in language, such as burstiness, large dictionaries and skewed rank-frequency distributions, control the trade-off or simultaneous appearance of these two forms of learning. We first show that these results are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network trained on a simplified dataset. In-context learning (ICL) is driven by the abrupt emergence of an induction head, which subsequently competes with in-weights learning. By identifying progress measures that precede in-context learning and targeted experiments, we construct a two-parameter model of an induction head which emulates the full data distributional dependencies displayed by the attention-based network. A phenomenological model of induction head formation traces its abrupt emergence to the sequential learning of three nested logits enabled by an intrinsic curriculum. We propose that the sharp transitions in attention-based networks arise due to a specific chain of multi-layer operations necessary to achieve ICL, which is implemented by nested nonlinearities sequentially learned during training.

papers.title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models handle knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and contextual information, and can we design a method to steer them towards either source without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads and proposes JUICE, a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: JUICE sets a new state-of-the-art for handling knowledge conflicts, offering robust generalization across domains and conflict types, and is supported by theoretical analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit inconsistent behaviors under different degrees of knowledge conflict, challenging the notion of exclusive 'memory heads' and 'context heads'.
Combining individually effective interventions can lead to counteracting effects due to superposition.
JUICE achieves state-of-the-art performance in steering LMs towards parametric or contextual knowledge across diverse datasets and models.
JUICE is effective even with a very small head identification set (e.g., 4 samples).
The dual-run design of JUICE mitigates superposition effects and outperforms single-run interventions.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often encounter knowledge conflicts when parametric memory contradicts contextual knowledge. Previous works attribute this conflict to the interplay between "memory heads" and "context heads", attention heads assumed to promote either memory or context exclusively. In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. Building upon this insight, we propose Just Run Twice (JuICE), a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without requiring fine-tuning. JuICE identifies a set of reliable attention heads and leverages a dual-run approach to mitigate the superposition effects. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets and 6 model architectures demonstrate that JuICE sets the new state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization, achieving significant and consistent improvement across different domains under various conflict types. Finally, we theoretically analyze knowledge conflict and the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads, which further elucidates the effectiveness of JuICE in these settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/JUICE.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning Beyond Transformers: An Investigation of State Space and Hybrid Architectures
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work internally in state-space and hybrid architectures, and how do these mechanisms compare to transformers across different task types?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends the analysis of function vectors (FVs) to state-space and hybrid architectures, revealing that while models can exhibit similar ICL performance, their internal mechanisms differ, with FVs being more critical for parametric knowledge retrieval than contextual understanding.
papers.conclusion: The work extends prior analysis of function vectors to diverse architectures and contributes to a more nuanced understanding of FVs across task types, while methodologically highlighting the importance of combining behavioral and mechanistic analyses.
papers.key_findings:
While LLMs of different architectures can behave similarly in task performance, their internal mechanisms can remain different.
Function vectors (FVs) responsible for ICL are primarily located in the self-attention and Mamba layers.
Mamba2 appears to use a different mechanism from FVs to perform ICL.
FVs are more important for ICL involving parametric knowledge retrieval than for contextual knowledge understanding.
In hybrid models, ICL capabilities are primarily contributed by FVs located in self-attention layers, regardless of whether self-attention and SSM layers are stacked in parallel or sequentially.
papers.abstract: We perform in-depth evaluations of in-context learning (ICL) on state-of-the-art transformer, state-space, and hybrid large language models over two categories of knowledge-based ICL tasks. Using a combination of behavioral probing and intervention-based methods, we have discovered that, while LLMs of different architectures can behave similarly in task performance, their internals could remain different. We discover that function vectors (FVs) responsible for ICL are primarily located in the self-attention and Mamba layers, and speculate that Mamba2 uses a different mechanism from FVs to perform ICL. FVs are more important for ICL involving parametric knowledge retrieval, but not for contextual knowledge understanding. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding across architectures and task types. Methodologically, our approach also highlights the importance of combining both behavioural and mechanistic analyses to investigate LLM capabilities.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning from Repetitions
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism underpinning in-context learning in Large Language Models, and how can it be understood through the lens of surface repetitions and token co-occurrence reinforcement?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel feature-centric perspective on in-context learning by identifying and analyzing token co-occurrence reinforcement, showing how surface patterns both enable and hinder ICL.
papers.conclusion: Token reinforcement is a key mechanism in in-context learning, acting as a double-edged sword that can be leveraged to maximize ICL effectiveness with informed demonstrations.
papers.key_findings:
Token co-occurrence reinforcement exists: the connection between any two tokens strengthens with their contextual co-occurrences.
Token reinforcement helps constrain the output space and enables models to follow patterns like chain-of-thought prompting.
Token reinforcement can lead to spurious connections and cause ICL failures when demonstrations contain unintended patterns.
The reinforcement effect scales with model size, with larger models showing stronger distant reinforcement.
Token reinforcement arises from the model's optimization of training likelihood, as evidenced by empirical analysis of pretraining data.
papers.abstract: This paper explores the elusive mechanism underpinning in-context learning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Our work provides a novel perspective by examining in-context learning via the lens of surface repetitions. We quantitatively investigate the role of surface features in text generation, and empirically establish the existence of \emph{token co-occurrence reinforcement}, a principle that strengthens the relationship between two tokens based on their contextual co-occurrences. By investigating the dual impacts of these features, our research illuminates the internal workings of in-context learning and expounds on the reasons for its failures. This paper provides an essential contribution to the understanding of in-context learning and its potential limitations, providing a fresh perspective on this exciting capability.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Probing Latent Knowledge Conflict for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How can we improve contextual faithfulness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by moving beyond black-box interventions and analyzing the model's internal reasoning process? Specifically, how is conflict represented in the model's latent space and how does it disrupt faithful generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ProbeRAG, a framework that leverages latent probing to detect knowledge conflicts in the model's hidden states and uses conflict-aware attention modulation to improve contextual faithfulness in RAG systems.
papers.conclusion: ProbeRAG effectively improves contextual faithfulness in RAG by moving beyond black-box interventions to internal guidance, demonstrating consistent and robust performance across various models and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting and aligned knowledge states are linearly separable in the model's latent space, providing a detectable 'conflict feature'.
Contextual noise systematically increases the entropy of these representations, obscuring the conflict feature.
ProbeRAG, which integrates fine-grained knowledge pruning, latent conflict probing, and conflict-aware attention, substantially improves accuracy and contextual faithfulness across multiple benchmarks and models.
The accuracy of the conflict probe is positively correlated with the model's ability to generate faithful responses.
Attention visualization shows that after training with the attention-guidance loss, the model allocates more attention to tokens marked as conflicting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to enhance the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing RAG systems often suffer from an unfaithfulness issue, where the model's response contradicts evidence from the retrieved context. Existing approaches to improving contextual faithfulness largely rely on external interventions, such as prompt engineering, decoding constraints, or reward-based fine-tuning. These works treat the LLM as a black box and overlook a crucial question: how does the LLM internally integrate retrieved evidence with its parametric memory, particularly under knowledge conflicts? To address this gap, we conduct a probing-based analysis of hidden-state representations in LLMs and observe three findings: knowledge integration occurs hierarchically, conflicts manifest as latent signals at the sentence level, and irrelevant context is often amplified when aligned with parametric knowledge. Building on these findings, we propose CLEAR (Conflict-Localized and Enhanced Attention for RAG), a framework that (i) decomposes context into fine-grained sentence-level knowledge, (ii) employs hidden-state probing to localize conflicting knowledge, and (iii) introduces conflict-aware fine-tuning to guide the model to accurately integrate retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR substantially improves both accuracy and contextual faithfulness, consistently outperforming strong baselines under diverse conflict conditions. The related resources are available at https://github.com/LinfengGao/CLEAR.

papers.title: Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do distributional and mechanistic factors determine a language model's behavior when there is a conflict between memorized facts and in-context information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies specific attention heads that control the use of memorized vs. in-context information and shows that scaling these heads at runtime can dynamically control model behavior without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that frequency and specific attention heads influence factual recall and provides a proof of concept for controlling model behavior dynamically at runtime.
papers.key_findings:
The frequency of the country and in-context city in pretraining data affects the model's tendency to use memorized vs. in-context information.
Larger models are more likely to use memorized answers, especially for frequent terms.
Individual attention heads can be identified that promote either memorized or in-context answers.
Scaling down a memory head can increase the rate of in-context answers to 88% on the world capitals task.
The memory head promotes geography-related tokens, indicating domain specificity, and does not generalize well to other factual domains.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: Linking In-context Learning in Transformers to Human Episodic Memory
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between induction heads in Transformer models and human episodic memory, specifically the Contextual Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that induction heads in Transformers are behaviorally, functionally, and mechanistically similar to the CMR model of human episodic memory, and that CMR-like heads emerge in intermediate to late layers and causally contribute to in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The study uncovers a parallel between the computational mechanisms of large language models and human memory, offering insights for both AI and neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in GPT2-small show attention biases (temporal contiguity and forward asymmetry) similar to human episodic memory.
The CMR model can be mapped to a Q-composition induction head, revealing mechanistic similarities.
CMR-like heads (with low CMR distance) are found in intermediate to late layers of various LLMs (GPT2, Pythia, Qwen, Mistral, Llama).
In Pythia models, CMR-like heads develop human-like temporal clustering over training.
Ablation of CMR-like heads reduces in-context learning performance, indicating a causal role.
papers.limitation:
It is unclear if CMR can serve as a mechanistic model in larger Transformer models.
It is unclear if the conclusions hold for untested Transformer models.
The causal analysis lacks the power to narrow down the causal role of specific CMR-like characteristics.
A systematic evaluation using specific datasets and tasks would allow for a stronger causal claim.
future_direction: Addressing the limitations by testing if CMR can serve as a mechanistic model in larger Transformers.
Testing the conclusions on more Transformer models.
Conducting systematic evaluation with specific datasets and tasks to strengthen causal claims.
papers.abstract: Understanding connections between artificial and biological intelligent systems can reveal fundamental principles of general intelligence. While many artificial intelligence models have a neuroscience counterpart, such connections are largely missing in Transformer models and the self-attention mechanism. Here, we examine the relationship between interacting attention heads and human episodic memory. We focus on induction heads, which contribute to in-context learning in Transformer-based large language models (LLMs). We demonstrate that induction heads are behaviorally, functionally, and mechanistically similar to the contextual maintenance and retrieval (CMR) model of human episodic memory. Our analyses of LLMs pre-trained on extensive text data show that CMR-like heads often emerge in the intermediate and late layers, qualitatively mirroring human memory biases. The ablation of CMR-like heads suggests their causal role in in-context learning. Our findings uncover a parallel between the computational mechanisms of LLMs and human memory, offering valuable insights into both research fields.

papers.title: Provable Low-Frequency Bias of In-Context Learning of Representations
papers.research_question: How does the double convergence process in in-context learning lead to an implicit bias towards smooth (low-frequency) representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the double convergence framework to explain the low-frequency bias in in-context learning, providing theoretical explanations for several empirical phenomena.
papers.conclusion: The double convergence phenomenon leads to a low-frequency bias in in-context learning, explaining several observed phenomena and providing a theoretical foundation for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Double convergence (context-wise and layer-wise) leads to an implicit low-frequency bias in hidden representations.
Explains why in-context learning can suppress the original semantic meaning learned during pre-training.
Explains why learned representations form a globally structured but locally distorted geometry.
Explains why the energy of representations decays but does not converge to zero.
Predicts and empirically verifies that in-context learning exhibits intrinsic robustness to high-frequency noise in the input.
papers.limitation: The most detailed results focus on the specific data-generating process (random walk on a graph) from Park et al. (2024), and generalizing to broader data distributions remains an open direction.
future_direction: Generalizing the analysis to broader data distributions.
Analyzing how the structural assumptions on attention maps emerge from pre-training.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to acquire new behaviors from the input sequence alone without any parameter updates. Recent studies have shown that ICL can surpass the original meaning learned in pretraining stage through internalizing the structure the data-generating process (DGP) of the prompt into the hidden representations. However, the mechanisms by which LLMs achieve this ability is left open. In this paper, we present the first rigorous explanation of such phenomena by introducing a unified framework of double convergence, where hidden representations converge both over context and across layers. This double convergence process leads to an implicit bias towards smooth (low-frequency) representations, which we prove analytically and verify empirically. Our theory explains several open empirical observations, including why learned representations exhibit globally structured but locally distorted geometry, and why their total energy decays without vanishing. Moreover, our theory predicts that ICL has an intrinsic robustness towards high-frequency noise, which we empirically confirm. These results provide new insights into the underlying mechanisms of ICL, and a theoretical foundation to study it that hopefully extends to more general data distributions and settings.

papers.title: Understanding the Interplay between Parametric and Contextual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models integrate their internal parametric knowledge with external contextual knowledge to solve complex problems?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs tend to suppress their internal parametric knowledge when contextual knowledge is available, even when it is complementary or irrelevant, and while instructions can encourage more reliance on internal knowledge, they still struggle to fully leverage it.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a key vulnerability in LLMs' ability to integrate parametric and contextual knowledge, raising concerns about their reliability in knowledge-intensive tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs universally suppress their parametric knowledge in the presence of contextual knowledge, regardless of model, knowledge type, or reasoning type.
LLMs are more likely to recall their knowledge for commonsense knowledge compared to scientific or factual knowledge, likely due to training corpus imbalance.
Explicit instructions can help LLMs remember more parametric knowledge, but they are still far from fully leveraging it.
LLMs rarely trust their own knowledge when faced with conflicting contextual knowledge, adhering to the context instead.
Instructions significantly influence LLMs' preferences towards their internal knowledge, but they still struggle to fully recall it in conflicting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) encode vast amounts of knowledge during pre-training (parametric knowledge, or PK) and can further be enhanced by incorporating contextual knowledge (CK). Can LLMs effectively integrate their internal PK with external CK to solve complex problems? In this paper, we investigate the dynamic interaction between PK and CK, categorizing their relationships into four types: Supportive, Complementary, Conflicting, and Irrelevant. To support this investigation, we introduce ECHOQA, a benchmark spanning scientific, factual, and commonsense knowledge. Our results show that LLMs tend to suppress their PK when contextual information is available, even when it is complementary or irrelevant. While tailored instructions can encourage LLMs to rely more on their PK, they still struggle to fully leverage it. These findings reveal a key vulnerability in LLMs, raising concerns about their reliability in knowledge-intensive tasks. Resources are available at https://github.com/sitaocheng/Knowledge_Interplay

papers.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Whether in-context learning and activation steering are instances of a broader framework for controlling LLM behavior, and how they jointly affect model behavior.
papers.core_contribution: Presents a Bayesian belief dynamics model that unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior under both interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian belief dynamics model unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior and revealing a phase boundary between interventions.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning and activation steering jointly affect behavior, creating a phase boundary modulated by context and activations.
The Bayesian model predicts sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates and additivity of interventions in log-belief space.
The model predicts crossover points (N*) where behavior transitions between concepts, with high correlation to empirical data.
The linear representation hypothesis holds within a range of steering magnitudes, beyond which behavior breaks down.
The model generalizes across different LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (persona, sentiment).
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis breaks down with large steering magnitudes, leading to chance behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be controlled at inference time through prompts (in-context learning) and internal activations (activation steering). Different accounts have been proposed to explain these methods, yet their common goal of controlling model behavior raises the question of whether these seemingly disparate methodologies can be seen as specific instances of a broader framework. Motivated by this, we develop a unifying, predictive account of LLM control from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, we posit that both context- and activation-based interventions impact model behavior by altering its belief in latent concepts: steering operates by changing concept priors, while in-context learning leads to an accumulation of evidence. This results in a closed-form Bayesian model that is highly predictive of LLM behavior across context- and activation-based interventions in a set of domains inspired by prior work on many-shot in-context learning. This model helps us explain prior empirical phenomena - e.g., sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates - while predicting novel ones - e.g., additivity of both interventions in log-belief space, which results in distinct phases such that sudden and dramatic behavioral shifts can be induced by slightly changing intervention controls. Taken together, this work offers a unified account of prompt-based and activation-based control of LLM behavior, and a methodology for empirically predicting the effects of these interventions.

papers.title: A Theory of Emergent In-Context Learning as Implicit Structure Induction
papers.research_question: When and how does in-context learning (ICL) emerge from generic next-token prediction in language models? The paper investigates the conditions under which ICL capabilities arise from the recombination of compositional operations found in natural language pretraining data.
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical framework showing that in-context learning emerges from next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient compositional structure, and validates this with experiments showing ICL emergence in scaled transformer LMs.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in language models arises from the recombination of compositional structure found in linguistic data, and the paper provides a theoretical and empirical step towards understanding this emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning emerges when scaling model parameters and data on compositionally structured pretraining distributions.
Prompting models to output intermediate steps (chain-of-thought) provides a theoretical and empirical benefit over direct prompting.
The success of ICL depends on the complexity of the task's compositional description and the iteration complexity of the pretraining data structure.
Probing experiments indicate that in-context learning is supported by the model learning a representation of the input's compositional structure.
The theoretical bounds are independent of the size of the object universe |Ω|, and empirical performance can even improve with larger |Ω|.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis considers an idealized predictor with infinite data and capacity, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world finite transformer models.
future_direction: Exploring more complex compositional structures and their learnability.
Investigating the application of the theory to real-world natural language data and models.
Extending the analysis to longer chains of reasoning and more complex task compositions.
papers.abstract: Scaling large language models (LLMs) leads to an emergent capacity to learn in-context from example demonstrations. Despite progress, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. We argue that in-context learning relies on recombination of compositional operations found in natural language data. We derive an information-theoretic bound showing how in-context learning abilities arise from generic next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient amounts of compositional structure, under linguistically motivated assumptions. A second bound provides a theoretical justification for the empirical success of prompting LLMs to output intermediate steps towards an answer. To validate theoretical predictions, we introduce a controlled setup for inducing in-context learning; unlike previous approaches, it accounts for the compositional nature of language. Trained transformers can perform in-context learning for a range of tasks, in a manner consistent with the theoretical results. Mirroring real-world LLMs in a miniature setup, in-context learning emerges when scaling parameters and data, and models perform better when prompted to output intermediate steps. Probing shows that in-context learning is supported by a representation of the input's compositional structure. Taken together, these results provide a step towards theoretical understanding of emergent behavior in large language models.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Simulated Adoption: Decoupling Magnitude and Direction in LLM In-Context Conflict Resolution
papers.research_question: Does the suppression of parametric knowledge in the residual stream arise from the radial dilution of the signal's magnitude, or from an angular displacement induced by orthogonal interference?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs resolve in-context knowledge conflicts through orthogonal interference in the residual stream, rotating hidden states rather than diluting signal magnitude, challenging scalar confidence metrics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs resolve knowledge conflicts via orthogonal interference in the residual stream, simulating adoption without erasing internal knowledge, highlighting the need for vectorial monitoring over scalar metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Logit decay for correct tokens occurs under conflicting contexts, most pronounced in final layers.
Norm dynamics vary by architecture; Llama-3.1-8B shows dilution, but Qwen-3-4B and GLM-4-9B maintain stable norms.
Interference vectors are quasi-orthogonal to truth directions, supporting the orthogonal interference hypothesis.
Angular deviation correlates strongly with performance drop, indicating geometric rotation is the dominant mechanism.
Compliance is characterized by simulated adoption, where internal truth is bypassed, not erased.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, assuming truth and context interact as linear vectors.
Dataset scope restricted to fact-based QA tasks (MMLU), may not generalize to other tasks.
Focus on final residual state before unembedding, not layer-wise evolution of interference vectors.
Sample size of three architectures may not capture behaviors of larger or MoE models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently prioritize conflicting in-context information over pre-existing parametric memory, a phenomenon often termed sycophancy or compliance. However, the mechanistic realization of this behavior remains obscure, specifically how the model resolves these knowledge conflicts through compliance, and whether this suppression arises from signal magnitude dilution or directional geometric alteration within the residual stream. To resolve this, we conducted a layer-wise geometric analysis across Qwen-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GLM-4-9B, decomposing the residual stream updates induced by counter-factual contexts into radial (norm-based) and angular (cosine-based) components. Our empirical results reject the universality of the "Manifold Dilution" hypothesis, as two of the three architectures maintained stable residual norms despite exhibiting significant performance degradation on factual queries. Instead, we observed that compliance is consistently characterized by "Orthogonal Interference," where the conflicting context injects a steering vector that is quasi-orthogonal to the ground-truth direction, effectively rotating the hidden state representation. This suggests that models do not "unlearn" or suppress the magnitude of internal truths but rather employ a mechanism of geometric displacement to bypass the correct unembedding vector, effectively simulating adoption while preserving the original structural magnitude. These findings challenge scalar confidence metrics for detecting hallucinations and underscore the necessity of vectorial monitoring to distinguish between genuine knowledge integration and superficial in-context mimicry.

papers.title: Learning vs Retrieval: The Role of In-Context Examples in Regression with Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the underlying mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in Large Language Models? Specifically, to what extent do LLMs retrieve internal knowledge versus learn from in-context examples during regression tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a new hypothesis and evaluation framework for in-context learning (ICL), arguing that ICL in LLMs is not purely learning or knowledge retrieval but operates on a spectrum between the two, which can be controlled via prompt engineering. Demonstrates this through extensive regression experiments on realistic datasets.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in LLMs is best understood as a spectrum between learning from examples and retrieving internal knowledge. The balance can be controlled through prompt engineering, such as revealing feature names, to optimize performance for regression tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can effectively perform regression on realistic datasets using in-context examples.
The ICL mechanism is a combination of learning from examples and retrieving internal knowledge; this balance shifts based on factors like the number of examples and the presence of feature names.
Providing feature names (enabling knowledge retrieval) improves performance, especially with few in-context examples, making LLMs more data-efficient than classical ML models in low-data regimes.
Randomizing the ground truth values in examples significantly degrades performance, demonstrating that LLMs do learn from the output labels in the examples.
Adding more features generally improves performance, primarily enhancing knowledge retrieval rather than learning when many examples are provided.
papers.limitation:
Scope limited to regression tasks and three specific datasets.
Treats LLMs as black boxes; underlying neural mechanisms remain opaque.
Token limits of some LLMs constrained testing beyond 100 in-context examples and three features in certain combinations.
Challenging to distinguish data contamination from approximate knowledge retrieval.
future_direction: Investigate more regression (or classification) datasets with different characteristics to elaborate on the findings.
Integrate the black-box evaluation approach with interpretability techniques for a deeper understanding of ICL mechanisms.
Use datasets from regions beyond the primary training domain of LLMs to mitigate data contamination concerns.
papers.abstract: Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of being in-context learners. However, the underlying mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) is still a major research question, and experimental research results about how models exploit ICL are not always consistent. In this work, we propose a framework for evaluating in-context learning mechanisms, which we claim are a combination of retrieving internal knowledge and learning from in-context examples by focusing on regression tasks. First, we show that LLMs can solve real-world regression problems and then design experiments to measure the extent to which the LLM retrieves its internal knowledge versus learning from in-context examples. We argue that this process lies on a spectrum between these two extremes. We provide an in-depth analysis of the degrees to which these mechanisms are triggered depending on various factors, such as prior knowledge about the tasks and the type and richness of the information provided by the in-context examples. We employ three LLMs and utilize multiple datasets to corroborate the robustness of our findings. Our results shed light on how to engineer prompts to leverage meta-learning from in-context examples and foster knowledge retrieval depending on the problem being addressed.

papers.title: DYNAMICQA: Tracing Internal Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of intra-memory conflict on language models' ability to accept relevant context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that language models exhibit greater intra-memory conflict with dynamic facts, and these facts are harder to update with context, indicating challenges for retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that intra-memory conflict affects context utilization in LMs, and dynamic facts are more difficult to update, highlighting issues for RAG systems.
papers.key_findings:
LMs show higher intra-memory conflict for dynamic facts compared to static facts.
Dynamic facts are harder to update with context, leading to more stubborn instances.
Semantic entropy does not reliably predict persuasion by context.
Temporality has a stronger negative correlation with persuasion than popularity or semantic entropy.
Llama-2 has the highest accuracy and persuasion but also the highest entropy among the models tested.
future_direction: Developing better measures for intra-memory conflict
Exploring other indicators of context use in RAGs
papers.abstract: Knowledge-intensive language understanding tasks require Language Models (LMs) to integrate relevant context, mitigating their inherent weaknesses, such as incomplete or outdated knowledge. However, conflicting knowledge can be present in the LM's parameters, termed intra-memory conflict, which can affect a model's propensity to accept contextual knowledge. To study the effect of intra-memory conflict on an LM's ability to accept relevant context, we utilize two knowledge conflict measures and a novel dataset containing inherently conflicting data, DynamicQA. This dataset includes facts with a temporal dynamic nature where facts can change over time and disputable dynamic facts, which can change depending on the viewpoint. DynamicQA is the first to include real-world knowledge conflicts and provide context to study the link between the different types of knowledge conflicts. We also evaluate several measures on their ability to reflect the presence of intra-memory conflict: semantic entropy and a novel coherent persuasion score. With our extensive experiments, we verify that LMs exhibit a greater degree of intra-memory conflict with dynamic facts compared to facts that have a single truth value. Furthermore, we reveal that facts with intra-memory conflict are harder to update with context, suggesting that retrieval-augmented generation will struggle with the most commonly adapted facts.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Secretly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning in GPT models? The paper investigates whether in-context learning can be understood as a form of implicit finetuning.
papers.core_contribution: The paper explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning by showing a dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, and provides empirical evidence that ICL behaves similarly to explicit finetuning.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning can be understood as a process of meta-optimization, specifically as implicit finetuning, and this understanding can inspire improved model designs like momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent.
In-context learning updates attention outputs and weights in a direction similar to explicit finetuning.
In-context learning covers most of the correct predictions made by a finetuned model.
In-context learning and finetuning pay similar attention to training tokens.
A momentum-based attention mechanism, inspired by the dual form, improves performance over vanilla attention in language modeling and ICL tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based architectures and does not cover other architectures like LSTMs.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard Transformer attention may be more complex.
Due to computational cost, the analysis is limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and does not include larger models.
The analysis is based only on classification tasks and does not consider other task types like multiple choice or open-ended generation.
future_direction: Study in-context learning in non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models (e.g., GPT 13B).
Investigate in-context learning on other task types like multiple choice and open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at https://aka.ms/icl.

papers.title: Distributional Associations vs In-Context Reasoning: A Study of Feed-forward and Attention Layers
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between feed-forward and attention layers in transformers regarding distributional associations and in-context reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Feed-forward layers in transformers learn distributional associations (e.g., bigrams) early in training, while attention layers learn in-context reasoning; truncating feed-forward layers can improve reasoning performance by removing distributional biases.
papers.conclusion: Distributional associations and in-context reasoning mechanisms are learned during training and tend to be disentangled in different parts of the model, such that selectively removing feed-forward components can lead to better predictions in reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Feed-forward layers quickly learn distributional associations (e.g., trigger-noise association) in early training steps.
Attention layers learn to attend to in-context targets and avoid noise tokens.
In models without feed-forward layers, the noise association is stored in a low-rank subspace of the value matrix.
Truncating feed-forward layers (e.g., via LASER) in pre-trained models improves performance on reasoning tasks by reducing distributional biases.
Theoretical analysis shows that gradients for feed-forward layers are less noisy and thus learn distributional associations faster.
papers.abstract: Large language models have been successful at tasks involving basic forms of in-context reasoning, such as generating coherent language, as well as storing vast amounts of knowledge. At the core of the Transformer architecture behind such models are feed-forward and attention layers, which are often associated to knowledge and reasoning, respectively. In this paper, we study this distinction empirically and theoretically in a controlled synthetic setting where certain next-token predictions involve both distributional and in-context information. We find that feed-forward layers tend to learn simple distributional associations such as bigrams, while attention layers focus on in-context reasoning. Our theoretical analysis identifies the noise in the gradients as a key factor behind this discrepancy. Finally, we illustrate how similar disparities emerge in pre-trained models through ablations on the Pythia model family on simple reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Fine-tuning for In-context Learning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently fine-tune language models for in-context learning by directly controlling the attention scores of induction heads, instead of using end-to-end fine-tuning with massive data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Attention Behavior Fine-Tuning (ABFT), an efficient fine-tuning method for in-context learning that directly optimizes attention scores of induction heads, and shows that this objective is implicit in end-to-end fine-tuning, suggesting a path toward mechanistic controllability.
papers.conclusion: ABFT effectively improves ICL performance by targeting induction heads, and the work demonstrates the potential of controlling model behavior through mechanistic interpretability, opening up the future application of mechanistic controllability.
papers.key_findings:
ABFT significantly improves ICL performance with high efficiency, using only around 0.01% of the data compared to previous methods.
ABFT improves prediction consistency against prompt template and demonstration sampling variations, and reduces bias towards seen labels in unseen-label scenarios.
ABFT is more efficient in time and memory and causes less harm to out-of-domain performance compared to end-to-end fine-tuning.
The ABFT objective is implicitly contained in the end-to-end training objective on ICL-style data, suggesting that such data naturally evokes induction heads.
ABFT demonstrates the possibility of controlling model behavior through intermediate features (attention scores) without supervising the final output, a step toward mechanistic controllability.
papers.limitation:
The induction head-based explanation and ABFT apply only to classification tasks with a finite label set; extending to open-ended tasks remains an open challenge.
The control methods based on gradients and moderate amounts of data are still coarse; future work could focus on gradient-free and data-free model editing.
future_direction: Extending the method to open-ended tasks.
Developing gradient-free and data-free model editing for better mechanistic controllability.
Further improving efficiency by restricting gradient updates to specific transformer layers and automatically optimizing hyperparameters and the induction head filter.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) utilizes structured demonstration-query inputs to induce few-shot learning on Language Models (LMs), which are not originally pre-trained on ICL-style data. To bridge the gap between ICL and pre-training, some approaches fine-tune LMs on large ICL-style datasets by an end-to-end paradigm with massive computational costs. To reduce such costs, in this paper, we propose Attention Behavior Fine-Tuning (ABFT), utilizing the previous findings on the inner mechanism of ICL, building training objectives on the attention scores instead of the final outputs, to force the attention scores to focus on the correct label tokens presented in the context and mitigate attention scores from the wrong label tokens. Our experiments on 9 modern LMs and 8 datasets empirically find that ABFT outperforms in performance, robustness, unbiasedness, and efficiency, with only around 0.01% data cost compared to the previous methods. Moreover, our subsequent analysis finds that the end-to-end training objective contains the ABFT objective, suggesting the implicit bias of ICL-style data to the emergence of induction heads. Our work demonstrates the possibility of controlling specific module sequences within LMs to improve their behavior, opening up the future application of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Illusion or Algorithm? Investigating Memorization, Emergence, and Symbolic Processing in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the extent to which in-context learning (ICL) in language models reflects true generalization versus memorization, and how ICL abilities and mechanisms develop during pre-training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that in-context learning (ICL) is not purely memorization nor purely symbolic algorithmic processing, and reveals predictable development patterns for complex ICL tasks linked to internal subspace allocation in the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that ICL is a mix of generalization and memorization, with predictable development for complex tasks, and internal mechanistic analysis reveals consistent subspace allocation patterns that advance understanding of ICL.
papers.key_findings:
LMs can perform pattern-based ICL tasks with random tokens, indicating generalization beyond memorization, but performance declines with rarer tokens, contradicting a pure symbolic algorithm view.
Different aspects of ICL develop idiosyncratically with model scale and training time, with performance gaps due to task configuration persisting while token frequency gaps stabilize.
The dimensionality of the residual stream subspace used for ICL follows a consistent pattern: an initial rise then decay, and development correlates with using a common subspace across tasks.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited by the availability of fine-grained checkpoints, particularly between steps 512 and 1000 in Pythia training, which could provide further insights.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more fine-grained checkpoint intervals.
Applying the SUDA method to a wider range of tasks in interpretability.
Systematic investigation across diverse factual and reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large-scale Transformer language models (LMs) trained solely on next-token prediction with web-scale data can solve a wide range of tasks after seeing just a few examples. The mechanism behind this capability, known as in-context learning (ICL), remains both controversial and poorly understood. Some studies argue that it is merely the result of memorizing vast amounts of data, while others contend that it reflects a fundamental, symbolic algorithmic development in LMs. In this work, we introduce a suite of investigative tasks and a novel method to systematically investigate ICL by leveraging the full Pythia scaling suite, including interim checkpoints that capture progressively larger amount of training data.
